BIE task prefix understand.read_page/3 · rulebook content_types@2026-10-24.1+explanations@2026-10-24.1+level_profiles@2026-10-24.1+simple_hindi@2026-10-23.4+teacher_examples@2026-10-24.1+vision-2026-10-21@2026-10-21.12 · content types 2026-10-24.1 · schema bie.brain.understand-page/3

You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (simple Hindi in Devanagari,
    the English term in Roman: "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"), everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

p0003-b0001 | Science and Technology
p0003-b0002 | There are mainly four different types of tissues present in our body.
p0003-b0003 | 1. Epithelial- provides covering or lining
p0003-b0004 | 2. Muscular- helps in movement
p0003-b0005 | 3. Neural- responds to stimuli
p0003-b0006 | 4. Connective- supports, links and cushions
p0003-b0007 |  Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body.
p0003-b0008 |  It also forms a barrier to keep different body systems separate.
p0003-b0009 |  Epithelial tissue cells are tightly packed and form a continuous sheet.
p0003-b0010 |  They have only a small amount of cementing material between them and
p0003-b0011 | almost no intercellular spaces.
p0003-b0012 |  All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an
p0003-b0013 | extracellular fibrous basement membrane.
p0003-b0014 |  Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which
p0003-b0015 | can secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the

output.page_summary: Four main body tissues are distinguished by function. Epithelium forms closely packed covering and lining sheets, rests on a basement membrane and may specialise into glands. Six epithelial types are compared by location, structure and function, with four illustrated examples.

items.content:
There are mainly four different types of tissues present in our body.
1. Epithelial- provides covering or lining
2. Muscular- helps in movement
3. Neural- responds to stimuli
4. Connective- supports, links and cushions

teacher_understanding.question: Which four main tissue types does the page identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial, muscular, neural and connective tissue form the four main groups listed here.

teacher_understanding.question: How do their main roles differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial tissue covers or lines; muscular tissue enables movement; neural tissue responds to stimuli; connective tissue supports, links and cushions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the body need these different kinds rather than one uniform tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Covering a surface, generating force, detecting changes and supporting parts demand different cell arrangements and activities. Division of work allows specialised tissues to perform these jobs effectively.

prerequisites: A tissue as a group of cells performing related functions
items.exam_note: Core matching and odd-one-out material: distinguish response to stimuli from movement and covering from support.

why_chain.step: The body needs surfaces protected, parts moved, changes detected and structures supported.
Different tissues divide these jobs rather than using the same structure for all of them.

unpack.example_or_place: Use the learner's arm: its covering, movement and response to touch illustrate different tissue jobs.
unpack.consequence: The remainder of this page examines the covering-and-lining group.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate four tissue roles around one body outline.
unpack.level_extra: Use function-based statement matching without assuming that a tissue has only one possible function.

items.content:
Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body.
It also forms a barrier to keep different body systems separate.

teacher_understanding.question: What physical role does epithelium play?
teacher_understanding.answer: It forms a covering or lining that also separates body compartments as a barrier.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page place these epithelial coverings?
teacher_understanding.answer: Over most organs and within body cavities.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a lining more than a passive wrapper?
teacher_understanding.answer: A continuous cellular boundary helps control contact and movement of materials between compartments; different linings can specialise for different exchanges.

items.exam_note: Covering, lining and separation are defining epithelial roles.

terms.plain_meaning: शरीर के भीतर की जगहें
terms.everyday_image: कमरे की अंदरूनी जगह

terms.plain_meaning: दो हिस्सों को अलग रखने वाली रोक
terms.everyday_image: दो कमरों के बीच दीवार

why_chain.step: Body compartments need boundaries so that their contents do not mix freely.
An epithelial covering provides a separating interface.

unpack.example_or_place: The digestive tract lining, listed later in the table, gives a familiar internal-surface example.
unpack.consequence: The next bullets explain the close packing that makes a sheet-like boundary possible.
unpack.visual_verb: Wrap an organ and line an internal space.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish an internal lining from a tissue lying deep beneath that lining.

items.where_on_page: upper middle, third and fourth bullets
items.content:
Epithelial tissue cells are tightly packed and form a continuous sheet.
They have only a small amount of cementing material between them and almost no intercellular spaces.

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement makes epithelium sheet-like?
teacher_understanding.answer: Closely packed cells, very little material between them and almost no intercellular spaces create a continuous cellular layer.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the small amount of cementing material situated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Between neighbouring epithelial cells rather than as a large space separating them.

teacher_understanding.question: How does close packing support the barrier role?
teacher_understanding.answer: Closely joined neighbouring cells reduce open gaps across a surface, like closely laid tiles. This supports a continuous boundary rather than a loose cellular mesh.

items.exam_note: A common distinguishing statement is scant intercellular material, not abundant matrix.

terms.plain_meaning: कोशिकाओं के बीच की खाली जगहें
terms.everyday_image: फर्श की टाइलों के बीच के अंतर

terms.plain_meaning: कोशिकाओं के बीच उन्हें साथ रखने में मदद करने वाला पदार्थ
terms.everyday_image: टाइलों के बीच थोड़ा सा जोड़ने वाला मसाला

why_chain.step: A boundary with many open gaps would not make an effective continuous covering.
Epithelial cells lie tightly together with little intervening material.

unpack.example_or_place: Visualise the mouth lining as closely arranged cells rather than widely scattered dots.
unpack.consequence: Cell arrangement explains how epithelium can cover and separate surfaces.
unpack.level_extra: Do not turn 'almost no spaces' into the claim that no material can cross epithelium.

items.content: All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the basement membrane described here?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is an extracellular fibrous layer separating epithelium from the tissue underneath.

teacher_understanding.question: Where should it be placed in a diagram?
teacher_understanding.answer: At the interface below the epithelial sheet and above the underlying tissue, not between every pair of epithelial cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does an epithelial sheet need a supporting interface?
teacher_understanding.answer: A surface sheet needs anchorage to the tissue below. The basement membrane provides support and attachment at that interface.

items.exam_note: Know the location and extracellular nature; do not confuse basement membrane with cell membrane.

terms.plain_meaning: कोशिका के बाहर स्थित
terms.everyday_image: घर के बाहर का रास्ता, घर का अंदरूनी कमरा नहीं

terms.plain_meaning: एपिथीलियम के नीचे की सहायक परत
terms.everyday_image: टाइलों के नीचे बिछा आधार

why_chain.step: A surface sheet needs attachment to the tissue beneath it.
The basement membrane provides a supporting interface below the epithelial cells.

unpack.example_or_place: In a tissue cross-section, locate the thin base immediately beneath the epithelial cells.
unpack.consequence: Separate the cellular epithelial sheet from its non-cellular supporting layer.
unpack.visual_verb: Lift the epithelial sheet to reveal its base.
unpack.level_extra: Preserve the book's qualifier 'usually'; avoid converting it into an unsupported absolute.

items.content: Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which can secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward, and a multicellular gland is formed. This is glandular epithelium.

teacher_understanding.question: What extra job can epithelial cells acquire?
teacher_understanding.answer: They can specialise as gland cells that release substances at an epithelial surface; this secretory specialisation is glandular epithelium.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page describe formation of a multicellular gland?
teacher_understanding.answer: A portion of the epithelial sheet folds inward, producing a gland made of multiple cells.

teacher_understanding.question: When is this inward-folding route relevant?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes it as something that happens sometimes during gland formation, not as a compulsory change in every epithelial sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is secretion a specialisation rather than simply covering?
teacher_understanding.answer: Secretion requires cells to produce or handle material and release it, adding an active chemical job to the physical job of making a surface.

items.exam_note: Link glandular epithelium to secretion and inward folding; distinguish absorption from secretion.

terms.plain_meaning: पदार्थ बनाकर या तैयार करके बाहर छोड़ना
terms.everyday_image: लार ग्रंथि से लार निकलना

terms.plain_meaning: कई कोशिकाओं से बनी स्राव करने वाली ग्रंथि
terms.everyday_image: कई काम करने वालों की एक छोटी उत्पादन इकाई

why_chain.step: Body surfaces may need useful substances delivered onto them.
Epithelial cells specialise for secretion, and an inward fold can form a multicellular gland.

unpack.example_or_place: Salivary glands provide a familiar secretion example; their ducts appear in the table.
unpack.consequence: Epithelium is not merely a passive covering; it can form secretory structures.
unpack.visual_verb: Fold a sheet inward and release droplets.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid treating 'sometimes' as 'all glands arise by this exact visible arrangement'.

items.where_on_page: upper right, four vertically stacked tissue drawings
items.content: Four separate epithelial tissue drawings show (a) a thin sheet of flat cells, (b) many stacked layers with flattened surface cells, (c) a single layer of cube-like cells, and (d) tall cells with cilia at their exposed surface. Each drawing rests on a contrasting basal strip. These are separate examples, not stages connected by arrows.
items.type_note: The image contains a teachable tissue figure, not non-teachable material.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the figure make visible?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contrasts flat, multilayered, cube-like and tall ciliated epithelial arrangements.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visual criteria distinguish the examples?
teacher_understanding.answer: Layer number distinguishes the stratified example, while cell shape and surface cilia distinguish the other drawings.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a learner identify these drawings rather than memorise their positions?
teacher_understanding.answer: First count layers, then inspect the surface cell shape, and finally look for projections such as cilia. This produces a reusable recognition method.

items.exam_note: Useful for diagram identification and matching appearance with tissue names.

terms.plain_meaning: ढकने या अस्तर बनाने वाली कोशिकाओं की परतें
terms.everyday_image: एक जैसी या कई मंज़िलों में लगी टाइलें

why_chain.step: Names alone can hide differences in tissue arrangement.
Count layers and compare cell shapes to recognise the illustrated types.

unpack.example_or_place: Compare the thin top drawing with the thick stratified block immediately below it.
unpack.consequence: The visual distinctions support the location–structure–function table.
unpack.visual_verb: Count layers and outline surface cells.
unpack.level_extra: The four pictures are examples, not an exhaustive classification or developmental sequence.

items.content: (a) Squamous — points to the thin sheet of flattened, irregularly outlined cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What appearance does the squamous label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: A thin sheet composed of flattened cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which drawing carries this label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The uppermost, very thin epithelial drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a floor-tile image useful here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tiles suggest broad, flat units placed side by side, helping distinguish squamous cells from cubes or pillars.

items.exam_note: Identify squamous by flattened cells, not by a compulsory number of layers.

terms.plain_meaning: चपटी कोशिकाओं वाला
terms.everyday_image: फर्श की सपाट टाइलें

unpack.example_or_place: The table places simple squamous tissue in lung air sacs.
unpack.consequence: Connect a flat cell shape with the thin exchange layer discussed below.
unpack.visual_verb: Flatten a cell into a tile.
unpack.level_extra: Squamous names shape; simple or stratified names layering.

items.content: (b) Stratified squamous — points to the thick block with many cell layers and flattened cells at the exposed surface.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: A multilayered epithelium whose upper cells are flattened.

teacher_understanding.question: Which feature separates it from the top drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: The visibly stacked layers rather than one thin sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are many layers useful on a worn surface?
teacher_understanding.answer: Surface cells can be lost while deeper layers continue to cover the underlying tissue.

items.exam_note: Name stratified epithelium by the surface cells, not necessarily by basal cell shape.

terms.plain_meaning: कई परतों में व्यवस्थित
terms.everyday_image: एक के ऊपर एक रखी चादरें

unpack.example_or_place: Mouth lining, listed in the table.
unpack.consequence: Multiple layers support protection despite surface wear.
unpack.visual_verb: Stack layers and highlight the flat top.
unpack.level_extra: A columnar lower layer does not make this stratified columnar tissue.

items.content: (c) Cuboidal — points to the single layer of cube-like epithelial cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What shape does cuboidal describe?
teacher_understanding.answer: The drawing shows cells with a roughly cube-like form rather than flattened or tall slender cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which image is cuboidal?
teacher_understanding.answer: The third drawing, showing a single row of relatively short, block-like cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a learner avoid confusing cuboidal with columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: Compare height with width: cuboidal cells are approximately as tall as wide, whereas columnar cells are noticeably taller.

items.exam_note: Recognise the cube-like form despite the table's imprecise 'short cylindrical' wording.

terms.plain_meaning: लगभग घन जैसी आकृति वाला
terms.everyday_image: खेल का पासा

unpack.consequence: Use shape recognition to connect the drawing to the cuboidal table row.
unpack.visual_verb: Compare a cube with a tall pillar.
unpack.level_extra: Approximate proportions matter; real cells need not be perfect geometric cubes.

items.content: (d) Columnar (Ciliated) — points to tall epithelial cells with a fringe of cilia on the exposed upper surface.

teacher_understanding.question: What two features does this label combine?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tall column-like cells and cilia at their exposed surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which feature indicates ciliated rather than merely columnar epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: The visible fringe of projections above the tall cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How do cilia assist surface movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated beating of these projections can move material along the epithelial surface.

items.exam_note: Cilia are a surface specialisation, not a separate layer of cells.

terms.plain_meaning: खंभे जैसी लंबी कोशिकाओं वाला
terms.everyday_image: इमारत के खंभे

terms.plain_meaning: सतह पर गति करने वाले महीन रेशों वाला
terms.everyday_image: एक दिशा में चलती छोटी झाड़ुओं की कतार

unpack.example_or_place: The columnar row links ciliation with movement in a specific direction.
unpack.consequence: Cell shape and surface specialisation must be read as separate features.
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer that every columnar epithelium is ciliated.

items.exam_note: Figure identifier only; content is captured in the diagram and labels.

items.exam_note: Six epithelial types are organised by location, structure and function; each row is captured below.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple squamous | Location: Blood vessel lining, capillaries, air sac lining of lungs, Bowman’s capsule of kidney | Structure: A single layer of flat cells having irregular boundaries | Function: Transport by diffusion and where minimal protection is required

teacher_understanding.question: What defines simple squamous structure?
teacher_understanding.answer: One layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries produces a thin epithelial sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the table locate it?
teacher_understanding.answer: In blood vessel lining and capillaries, the air sac lining of lungs and Bowman’s capsule of the kidney.

teacher_understanding.question: Which function is associated with this arrangement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table associates it with transport by diffusion and sites needing minimal protection.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a single flat layer suited to diffusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: Exchange needs a short crossing distance. A thin single layer reduces that distance compared with a thick stack of cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How does it differ from stratified squamous epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple squamous has one flat layer and is associated here with diffusion; stratified squamous has several layers and is associated with protection.

teacher_understanding.question: Should every listed location be taken to perform only diffusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. For example, the specialised lining associated with Bowman’s capsule participates in filtration. The table's broad diffusion entry should not erase location-specific functions.

items.exam_note: High-yield location matching; distinguish diffusion-friendly thinness from multilayer protection.

terms.plain_meaning: चपटी कोशिकाओं की एक परत
terms.everyday_image: फर्श पर टाइलों की एक पतली तह

terms.plain_meaning: कणों का अधिक सांद्रता से कम सांद्रता की ओर फैलना
terms.everyday_image: कमरे में इत्र की खुशबू फैलना

terms.plain_meaning: गुर्दे में छनने की शुरुआत से जुड़ी प्याले जैसी संरचना
terms.everyday_image: छनकर आए तरल को लेने वाला छोटा प्याला

why_chain.step: Exchange surfaces need substances to cross a short distance.
A single flattened cell layer provides a thin crossing barrier.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom from breathing lungs to the air sac lining; also locate capillaries and the kidney capsule.
unpack.consequence: Thinness suits exchange, whereas stronger wear protection is associated later with many layers.
unpack.visual_verb: Pass particles across one flattened layer.
unpack.level_extra: Do not equate all renal epithelial structures with the same type or function.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium | Location: The tubular lining of kidneys, glandular ducts | Structure: A single layer of short cylindrical cells. It may have microvilli as in proximal convoluted tubules | Function: Absorption and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What structure does the book assign to simple cuboidal epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes a single layer of short cylindrical cells, sometimes with microvilli, as in proximal convoluted tubules.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is it found according to the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: In kidney tubular lining and glandular ducts.

teacher_understanding.question: What functions are linked to it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Absorption and secretion: taking substances in and releasing substances are the two activities listed.

teacher_understanding.question: How do microvilli help an absorptive surface?
teacher_understanding.answer: These small surface projections enlarge the membrane area available for absorption without requiring a much larger organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the shape wording be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cuboidal conventionally means approximately as tall as wide. The printed phrase 'short cylindrical' is imprecise and should not be confused with tall columnar cells.

items.exam_note: Match kidney tubules and glandular ducts with simple cuboidal; microvilli increase absorption area, unlike motile cilia.

terms.plain_meaning: पदार्थ को सतह से अंदर लेना
terms.everyday_image: कागज़ का पानी सोखना

terms.plain_meaning: कोशिका की सतह के छोटे उभार जो क्षेत्रफल बढ़ाते हैं
terms.everyday_image: सीधी चादर को मोड़ने पर एक जगह अधिक सतह समाना

terms.plain_meaning: गुर्दे की छनन इकाई के शुरुआती घुमावदार नलिकीय हिस्से
terms.everyday_image: शुरुआत में मुड़ी हुई छोटी पाइप

why_chain.step: Kidney tubules need to recover useful substances from the fluid passing through them.
Microvilli enlarge the absorptive surface of suitable tubular cells.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom from the kidney to its small tubules; the proximal convoluted tubule is the microvilli example.
unpack.consequence: Surface modifications can enhance a tissue's function without changing its single-layer arrangement.
unpack.visual_verb: Enlarge a cell surface into microvilli and move substances across it.
unpack.level_extra: The book says 'may have': do not assign microvilli to every cuboidal epithelium.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Columnar Epithelium | Location: Digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining | Structure: A single layer of columnar cells (tall and slender) and often ciliated | Function: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement does simple columnar describe?
teacher_understanding.answer: A single layer of tall, slender cells; the table also notes that they are often ciliated.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations does this row give?
teacher_understanding.answer: Digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining.

teacher_understanding.question: What jobs does the row associate with these cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction.

teacher_understanding.question: How are mucus secretion and ciliary movement different jobs?
teacher_understanding.answer: Secretory cells release mucus, whereas beating cilia can move mucus and trapped material along a surface. Producing the material and moving it are distinct activities.

teacher_understanding.question: Should this row mean the entire upper respiratory tract is simple columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Much of the conducting respiratory tract has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, and some regions have other linings. The location entry is a broad simplification.

teacher_understanding.question: Are cilia and microvilli interchangeable?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Motile cilia move material along a surface, whereas microvilli primarily increase surface area for absorption.

items.exam_note: Distinguish tall shape, one layer and ciliation; avoid assuming every location performs every listed function.

why_chain.step: Internal passages need protection and handling of substances at their surfaces.
Columnar epithelial specialisations support absorption, secretion or directed surface movement according to the site.

unpack.example_or_place: Link digestive lining with taking in nutrients and respiratory cilia with moving mucus.
unpack.consequence: Cell shape alone does not specify every function; surface specialisation and location matter.
unpack.visual_verb: Raise tall cells, release mucus and sweep it in one direction.
unpack.level_extra: Treat the respiratory location cautiously; the next-page context introduces pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Squamous Epithelium | Location: The lining of the mouth and vagina | Structure: Made up of several layers of cells, continuously sloughed off and regenerated. The older layer of cells is pushed upwards and becomes flat. The lower layer is columnar and metabolically active | Function: Protection

teacher_understanding.question: What structural pattern defines this tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several cell layers lie above a metabolically active columnar lower layer; older cells move upward and flatten.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations are named?
teacher_understanding.answer: The mouth lining and vaginal lining.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page describe maintenance of the layers?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells are continuously sloughed off and regenerated, while older cells are pushed upward and become flat.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is renewal useful for a protective lining?
teacher_understanding.answer: Friction can remove exposed cells. Replacing them from deeper layers maintains a covering despite repeated wear.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a columnar basal layer not contradict the squamous name?
teacher_understanding.answer: Stratified epithelia are named according to the surface cell shape; the deeper cells can have a different shape.

items.exam_note: Strong location–protection match. Trap: basal cells are columnar but the superficial cells determine the squamous name.

why_chain.step: A lining exposed to repeated friction needs ongoing protection.
Several layers plus continual replacement preserve coverage as surface cells are lost.

unpack.example_or_place: The inside of the mouth experiences friction while food is chewed; vagina is the second listed site.
unpack.consequence: Protection is maintained by layered renewal rather than by the thin exchange design of simple squamous tissue.
unpack.visual_verb: Push cells upward, flatten them and shed the surface.
unpack.level_extra: Do not substitute skin for the page's stated examples; mouth and vagina are the listed locations.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Cuboidal | Location: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands | Structure: The upper layer is cuboid and other layers may be cuboidal or other types | Function: Protection of ducts of various glands

teacher_understanding.question: What structural feature gives stratified cuboidal its name?
teacher_understanding.answer: The upper layer is cuboid; deeper layers may also be cuboidal or may have other cell types.

teacher_understanding.question: Which glands are named in the location column?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands; the function column specifically identifies protection of gland ducts.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are duct linings relevant to this protective role?
teacher_understanding.answer: A duct carries gland products along a passage. Multiple epithelial layers can provide a more substantial protective lining than a single thin exchange layer.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this differ from simple cuboidal in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple cuboidal has one layer and is associated with absorption and secretion; stratified cuboidal has multiple layers and is associated here with duct protection.

items.exam_note: Match stratified cuboidal with gland duct protection; do not infer that an entire gland has one epithelial type.

terms.everyday_image: टंकी से पानी ले जाने वाली पाइप

why_chain.step: Gland products need a lined passage to travel through.
Stratified cuboidal tissue is linked here with protection of such ducts.

unpack.example_or_place: Sweat-gland ducts connect a familiar sweating experience with a protected gland passage.
unpack.consequence: Layer number distinguishes protective duct lining from simple cuboidal absorptive or secretory lining.
unpack.visual_verb: Line a gland duct with stacked cube-like cells.
unpack.level_extra: Location wording names glands broadly; keep attention on ducts rather than all secretory cells.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Columnar | Location: Male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands | Structure: There is a layer of columnar cells present on squamous, columnar or cuboidal epithelial cells | Function: Protection and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement defines this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: A columnar cell layer lies over epithelial cells that may be squamous, columnar or cuboidal.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page locate stratified columnar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands.

teacher_understanding.question: Which functions are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection and secretion.

teacher_understanding.question: How can deeper cells of different shapes still belong to stratified columnar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: The surface cells provide the shape term in the name, while 'stratified' records that more than one layer is present.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this differ from stratified cuboidal?
teacher_understanding.answer: The upper layer is columnar rather than cuboid; the table associates stratified columnar with both protection and secretion, and stratified cuboidal with duct protection.

items.exam_note: Location matching and surface-cell naming are important. Do not confuse urethra with ureter or assume the whole urethra has one lining.

why_chain.step: Some passages need a protective lining with secretory activity.
The table associates these jobs with stratified tissue having a columnar surface layer.

unpack.example_or_place: Trace saliva from the familiar salivary gland into its larger ducts; also locate the male urethra as an exit passage.
unpack.consequence: The six rows can be organised using two independent criteria: number of layers and surface cell shape.
unpack.visual_verb: Place tall cells on a deeper layer and trace a duct.
unpack.level_extra: Use exact location wording in matching questions; urethra is not the kidney-to-bladder ureter.
